_note: PLACEHOLDER CONTENT. Wording by the student team, not the text of VERBUND's competency model; only the grouping follows the structure shown in the team's jour fixe deck. Final profiles, levels and questions follow the interview data.

levels.name: Foundation
levels.short: Knows the basics and the rules

levels.name: Practitioner
levels.short: Applies it independently in the own job

levels.name: Advanced
levels.short: Shapes it for others and for the unit

competencies.name: Safe and compliant use
competencies.description: Uses approved AI tools within data protection, confidentiality and legal rules.
competencies.question: Which AI tools do you use in your work, and how do you decide what you may enter?
levels: Knows the approved tools and the rules for data and confidentiality.
Applies the rules in daily work without guidance and spots unclear cases.
Advises colleagues on unclear cases and helps to improve the rules.
competencies.why: Everyone who uses AI at work needs basic AI literacy; the EU AI Act asks companies to take measures for it.

examples.A: Decides which code and data may go into a coding assistant.
examples.B: Knows that contracts and personal data do not belong in a public chatbot.
examples.D: Uses only released tools for plant data and maintenance reports.
examples.M: Makes sure the team knows the rules and where to ask.

selfCheck.question: When you use AI at work, how do you decide which tools and data you may use?
answers: I am not sure which AI tools are approved or what I may enter.
I know the approved tools and which data must not go into them.
I follow the rules without having to look them up and notice when a case is unclear.
Colleagues come to me with unclear cases, and I suggest improvements to the rules.

selfCheck.question: What do you do when you are unsure whether you may use AI for a task?
answers: I have not been in this situation yet.
I ask someone before I go ahead.
I check the guideline myself and clarify open points with the right contact.
I help others to decide such cases and pass recurring questions on.

competencies.name: Critical review of results
competencies.description: Checks AI output for errors and bias and stays accountable for the result.
competencies.question: Tell me about a case where an AI result was wrong or incomplete. How did you notice?
levels: Knows that AI output can be wrong and checks facts before using it.
Verifies output systematically with sources, plausibility checks or a second person.
Defines quality checks for the team and trains others in them.
competencies.why: AI output can sound right and be wrong. Whoever uses it stays responsible for the result.

examples.A: Reviews and tests generated code before it is merged.
examples.B: Checks figures and sources of an AI-drafted report against the original data.
examples.D: Compares an AI fault diagnosis with measurements and own experience.
examples.M: Asks how a result was checked before deciding on it.

selfCheck.question: How do you check an AI result before you use it?
answers: I mostly use AI results as they are.
I check the facts that matter before I use a result.
I check results routinely, for example against sources or with a second person.
I have defined checks that my team uses, and I show others how to apply them.

selfCheck.question: What happens when an AI result is wrong or one-sided?
answers: I would probably not notice it.
I notice obvious errors and correct them.
I find less obvious errors and bias too, and I know where AI tends to fail in my work.
I collect typical errors and share them so that others can avoid them.

competencies.name: Identifying use cases
competencies.description: Recognises tasks in the own area where AI saves time or improves quality.
competencies.question: Where in your work would AI help most? What would it take to try it?
levels: Can name tasks in the own job that AI could support.
Describes a use case with benefit, data needed and risks.
Prioritises use cases for the unit and brings them into the decision process.
competencies.why: The best ideas for using AI come from the people who know the work.

examples.A: Sees where tests, documentation or monitoring can be supported by AI.
examples.B: Spots recurring reports or enquiries that an assistant could prepare.
examples.D: Suggests where inspection data could point to maintenance needs earlier.
examples.M: Collects ideas from the team and brings the best ones forward.

selfCheck.question: Can you name tasks in your job where AI would help?
answers: I cannot name one yet.
I can name some tasks AI could support.
I can describe a use case with its benefit, the data it needs and its risks.
I compare use cases for our unit and bring the best ones into the decision process.

selfCheck.question: What do you do with an idea for using AI?
answers: I have not had an idea like this yet.
I mention it to my manager or my team.
I try it out on a small scale and share what I learned.
I make sure good ideas are assessed and followed up across the unit.

competencies.name: Building and scaling solutions
competencies.description: Turns a use case into a working solution and makes it reusable.
competencies.question: Have you built or configured an AI solution yourself, for example a prompt template, an agent or an automation?
levels: Uses templates and solutions that others have built.
Builds simple solutions for the own work and shares them.
Develops solutions for several teams and takes care of operation and quality.
competencies.why: A use case only pays off once it runs and others can reuse it.

examples.A: Builds an agent or a pipeline and looks after operation and quality.
examples.B: Sets up a prompt template for a recurring report and shares it.
examples.D: Configures an assistant for standard maintenance documentation.
examples.M: Makes sure a working solution is handed over and reused in other teams.

selfCheck.question: Have you built an AI solution yourself, for example a prompt template, an agent or an automation?
answers: No, I have not used one so far.
I use templates and solutions others have built.
I build simple solutions for my own work and share them.
I develop solutions for several teams and take care of their operation and quality.

selfCheck.question: How do others benefit from what you build?
answers: I have not built anything to share yet.
I sometimes pass a good prompt or tip on.
I document my solutions so that colleagues can reuse them.
My solutions run for other teams, and I keep them up to date.

competencies.name: Steering AI use in the team
competencies.description: Sets goals and rules for AI use in the team and knows the AI levels of its members.
competencies.question: How do you decide where your team uses AI, and how do you follow what comes out of it?
levels: Knows where the team already uses AI.
Sets goals and priorities for AI use and reviews results regularly.
Aligns AI use with the unit's strategy and with data, process and project needs.
competencies.why: Managers decide where AI is used and answer for the results.

examples.M: Sets two or three AI goals for the team and reviews them every quarter.

selfCheck.question: How well do you know where your team uses AI?
answers: I do not really know yet.
I know where my team already uses AI.
I have set goals and priorities for AI use and review the results regularly.
I align our AI use with the unit's strategy and with data, process and project needs.

selfCheck.question: How do you see the AI skills of your team members?
answers: I have no picture of them yet.
I have a rough picture from daily work.
I know each person's level and plan development with them.
I use the team's levels to plan staffing and development across the unit.

competencies.name: Guiding the change
competencies.description: Leads by example, takes up concerns and gives the team time to learn.
competencies.question: What do you do so that all team members, also the hesitant ones, get started with AI?
levels: Uses AI visibly in the own work and talks about it.
Plans learning time, addresses concerns and uses role models in the team.
Builds a learning culture across teams and develops other managers.
competencies.why: Teams follow what managers do, not what they announce.

examples.M: Blocks learning time and shows the own use of AI in team meetings.

selfCheck.question: How visible is your own use of AI to your team?
answers: I hardly use AI myself yet.
I use AI in my own work and talk about it.
I show the team concrete examples and invite them to try things.
Other managers use my examples and approach in their teams.

selfCheck.question: What do you do for team members who are hesitant about AI?
answers: I have not done anything specific yet.
I listen to their concerns.
I plan learning time, address concerns and pair them with role models.
I help build a learning culture across teams and coach other managers in it.

families.name: Software, IT & Data
families.summary: Builds and runs the digital systems. Highest AI exposure and the role of multiplier.
families.example: e.g. coding assistants, automated testing, data pipelines with AI checks

families.name: Commercial & Corporate Office
families.summary: Finance, procurement, HR, legal and administration. Text- and data-heavy work.
families.example: e.g. report drafts, contract summaries, analysis of supplier data

families.name: Engineering & Technicians
families.summary: Plans, builds and maintains the plants. AI supports, physical work stays.
families.example: e.g. AI-supported CAD, simulation, maintenance and process analysis

families.name: Managers & Executives
families.summary: Separate group across all families: they lead the change and assess their teams.
families.example: e.g. team goals for AI use, competency conversations, learning time

measures.title: Basic training on approved tools and data rules
measures.description: Mandatory and repeated every year, with cases from the own unit.

measures.title: Workshop on checking AI output
measures.description: Real tasks from the team; a four-eyes check for critical results.

measures.title: Use-case workshop in the team
measures.description: Small groups work on use cases from their own job.

measures.title: Hands-on sessions on templates and agents
measures.description: Learning by doing on a real use case, with a mentor.

measures.title: Leadership programme on AI
measures.description: Steering AI use, leading the change, peer exchange between managers.

measures.title: Programme for changing roles
measures.description: For employees whose tasks change strongly, for example towards data or automation work.

measures.title: Hire for scarce advanced skills
measures.description: Where the gap to the advanced level cannot be closed in time by training.

measures.title: Target profile in job ads and selection
measures.description: The profile of the job family becomes part of job ads and interviews.

measures.title: AI champions in the units
measures.description: Role models who help colleagues and collect use cases.

measures.title: Fixed learning time
measures.description: Agreed hours per month in the team calendar.

measureTypes.name: Upskilling
measureTypes.short: Deepen skills in the current job

measureTypes.name: Reskilling
measureTypes.short: Prepare for a changed or new role

measureTypes.name: Organisation
measureTypes.short: Roles, time and structures that make learning stick

roadmap.title: Foundation
items: Target profiles for three job families and managers

roadmap.title: Pilot
items: Pilot in two or three units
Agreement with the works council on recording competencies
Review of profiles and guide after the pilot

roadmap.title: Roll-out
items: Competency conversations in all units of the focus families
Measures matched to the largest gaps

roadmap.title: Embedding
items: Part of the yearly appraisal cycle
Link to workforce planning and recruiting

roles.tasks: Maintains competencies, levels and target profiles; decides on changes.

roles.who: Digital unit, AI centre of enablement
roles.tasks: Reports new tools and use cases; proposes changes to the profiles.
Hold the competency conversation once a year and agree on levels.
Matches the learning offer to the largest gaps.
Agrees on what is recorded, who sees it and how long it is kept.

cycle.detail: Owner and digital unit check the targets against new tools and the strategy.
Managers and employees agree on levels.
HR reads the aggregated gaps; Learning & Development adjusts the offer.
What did the measures change? Input for the next review.

rules: The check serves development. It is not used for pay, appraisal or staffing decisions.
Levels are agreed by two people in a conversation. No AI rates anyone.
A manager sees the own team. HR sees totals only, never single persons.
Groups with fewer than five rated employees are not shown.
Employees can see everything stored about them and ask for corrections.
Entries are replaced by next year's conversation.
Purpose, access and retention are fixed in a works agreement (Betriebsvereinbarung) before any real use.
